claims.text: The as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a primarily metastable microstructure.
The initial metastable microstructure contains nanocrystalline or amorphous regions.
The initial alloy has minimal intermetallic-compound development.
Exposure to corrosive and high-temperature oxidative environments causes the metastable microstructure to evolve.
Environmental exposure promotes rapid Mg diffusion from the metastable microstructure.
Rapid Mg diffusion triggers phase separation.
Mg segregates to internal boundaries during environmental exposure.
Stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form and grow at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds alters local electrochemical potentials.
The altered local electrochemical potentials enhance local galvanic coupling.
Enhanced galvanic coupling increases susceptibility to localized corrosion.
After treatment, the alloy will exhibit a higher corrosion rate than in its as-processed state.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds enables a more uniform and protective oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
After treatment, the alloy will have improved high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to its as-processed state.
The proposed mechanism applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with density below 6 g/cm³.
The proposed mechanism requires exposure sufficiently aggressive to drive phase evolution without causing complete structural failure.
